reasons: No test or dry-run mode is visible in the file.
Company IDs are hardcoded, so the links depend on the database content staying the same.
Each reactor is saved separately with no transaction, so a crash can leave partial data.
The first grid connection date is stored in the commercial operation date field by design, which can mislead anyone reading that field.

terms.meaning: the IAEA Power Reactor Information System, a public database of nuclear reactors
the International Atomic Energy Agency, a UN body that publishes reactor data
commercial operation date, the date a plant starts selling power; this file stores first grid connection in that field
a library that lets code ask the database questions in TypeScript instead of raw SQL
a starter data file loaded into the system once or repeatedly
a record saying which company plays which role, such as owner or operator, in a project

used_by: None visible in the packet; the file appears to be run directly from the command line.

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Imports and file location setup
sections.what: Brings in the database connection, the project and company link table definitions, a nuclear classifier, and file tools. It also works out the folder the script lives in so it can find its data file.
sections.why: Likely reason: a script run outside the app needs its own connection and file path handling.
sections.watch_out: The data file is found relative to this folder, so moving the script also moves where it looks for data.

sections.name: PrisReactor
sections.title: The shape of one reactor record
sections.what: Describes the fields each PRIS reactor entry must have: IAEA id, name, country, reactor type, capacity, status, and two dates. A long comment records a decision that the grid date means first grid connection, not commercial operation.
sections.why: The comment states the decision and points to a reconciliation script and a country helper for the reasoning.
sections.watch_out: Readers of the commercial operation date field should know that for these rows it holds first grid connection.

sections.name: STATUS_MAP
sections.title: Turns PRIS status into project status
sections.what: Converts each PRIS status text into the app's project status and lifecycle stage. For example, an operational plant becomes on track and operating.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond the mapping itself; it translates outside wording into the app's terms.
sections.watch_out: Any status text not in this list is treated as planned by the main loop, so a new PRIS status can be recorded wrongly without an error.

sections.name: TECH_MAP
sections.title: Turns reactor family codes into names
sections.what: Converts PRIS reactor family codes into readable technology names, for example mapping the old graphite-channel code to RBMK.
sections.why: Likely reason: PRIS uses short codes that are not meant for display.
sections.watch_out: A code missing from this list is stored as it is, so an unfamiliar code shows up raw in the app.

sections.name: CompanyRule
sections.title: Shape of a company link rule
sections.what: Describes one rule: a company ID and the role that company plays for a project, such as owner or operator.
sections.why: Reason not stated; it is the data shape for the country map.
sections.watch_out: Roles are free text here, so a misspelled role creates a link that matches nothing.

sections.name: COUNTRY_COMPANY_MAP
sections.title: Default companies by country
sections.what: Lists which company IDs act as owners, operators, reactor vendors, or technology providers for each country. These rules are applied when company linking is switched on.
sections.why: Likely reason: most reactors in a country share the same owner or vendor, so one table fills many links.
sections.watch_out: The IDs are hardcoded, and the same ID appears under several countries and roles without explanation.

sections.name: CHINA_CGN_PATTERNS
sections.title: Name hints for a Chinese nuclear owner
sections.what: A list of plant name fragments that identify plants run by one Chinese nuclear group.
sections.why: Reason not stated; likely used to decide the owner from the plant's name.
sections.watch_out: Matching is a simple text search, so a short fragment could match an unrelated name.

sections.name: getChinaOwner, CANADA_BRUCE_PATTERNS
sections.title: Picks the owner for Chinese plants
sections.what: Checks a plant name against the list and returns one owner ID. If nothing matches, it returns a fallback owner ID. The Canada name list is also defined here.
sections.why: Reason not stated; the fallback appears to be a default owner.
sections.watch_out: Any plant not on the list is assigned the fallback owner without a warning.

sections.name: getCanadaOwner
sections.title: Picks the owner for Canadian plants
sections.what: Returns one fixed owner for Bruce plants and a different default owner for other Canadian plants.
sections.why: Likely reason: the Bruce plants have a different owner from the rest.
sections.watch_out: Only the word bruce is matched, so a renamed plant falls into the default owner.

sections.name: US_OPERATOR_MAP
sections.title: Maps US plant names to operators
sections.what: Lists name fragments for US reactor sites, each paired with an operator company ID.
sections.why: Likely reason: operator data is not in PRIS, so a manual list fills the gap.
sections.watch_out: Fragments are not checked for overlaps, and a plant missing from the list gets no operator.

sections.name: getUSOperator
sections.title: Finds the operator for a US plant
sections.what: Returns the operator ID for the first name fragment found in the plant's name, or nothing if none match.
sections.why: Reason not stated beyond the name matching itself.
sections.watch_out: The first match in the list wins, so overlapping names can pick the wrong operator.

sections.name: likelihood
sections.title: Gives a likelihood score by status
sections.what: Returns a score for how likely a project is to happen, based on its PRIS status. Operating plants get 80, under construction 70, planned 50, shut down 100, and anything else 30.
sections.why: Reason not stated; the numbers appear to be fixed judgments.
sections.watch_out: A shut-down plant scores 100, which reads as most certain in the app, and the code does not explain this.

sections.name: maturity
sections.title: Gives a maturity label by status
sections.what: Labels operating, under construction, and shut-down plants as bankable, planned plants as medium, and all others as low.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Shut-down plants are labeled bankable, which may confuse readers.

sections.name: normalizeForMatch
sections.title: Makes names comparable
sections.what: Lowercases a name and removes everything except letters and digits, so differently punctuated names can match.
sections.why: Likely reason: the same plant is often spelled with different spacing and punctuation across sources.
sections.watch_out: Names that differ only in punctuation are treated as the same, so two similar plants could be merged.

sections.name: getNextId
sections.title: Finds the next free project number
sections.what: Looks at existing project ids starting with p- and returns one more than the highest number.
sections.why: Likely reason: new projects need unique readable ids.
sections.watch_out: The number is worked out once at the start, so two runs at the same time could pick the same number.

sections.name: snakeToCamel
sections.title: Renames database columns to camel case
sections.what: Converts column names such as source_keys into sourceKeys, so the rest of the script uses the same names as the code.
sections.why: Likely reason: raw database queries return underscore names, while the code uses camel case.
sections.watch_out: It only changes names, not values, so it is safe but applies only to raw query results.

sections.name: findByIaeaKey
sections.title: Looks up a project by PRIS id
sections.what: Searches projects whose stored source keys include this PRIS number and returns the first match, with its names converted.
sections.why: Likely reason: the PRIS number is the most reliable way to recognize a plant already in the database.
sections.watch_out: The lookup only works if the stored source keys hold the PRIS number as text.

sections.name: upsertLink
sections.title: Adds or refreshes one company link
sections.what: If a link with the same company, project, and role exists, it updates the last-seen time. Otherwise it creates a new link with a confidence of 0.7.
sections.why: Likely reason: running the script again should not create duplicate links.
sections.watch_out: Every new link gets the same fixed confidence of 0.7, and the code does not say why.

sections.name: linkCompanies
sections.title: Links companies to one plant
sections.what: Applies the country table, then the China, Canada, and US owner or operator rules for the plant, and returns how many link attempts it made.
sections.why: Reason stated only by the rules themselves; the function groups all the linking in one place.
sections.watch_out: The count is of attempts, not of newly created links, so the final total can be higher than the new rows added.

sections.name: main (part 1)
sections.title: Starts the run and prepares each reactor
sections.what: Reads the command flags, prints a header, loads the seed file, and loads all existing projects into a lookup by name and country. For each reactor it works out status, technology, classification, and capacity, then looks for an existing match by PRIS id or by name and country.
sections.why: Likely reason: loading everything once avoids a database query for each name match.
sections.watch_out: The name lookup is built before the loop, so a project added during the run is only found later if it is also added to that lookup.

sections.name: main: if
sections.title: Updates a plant already in the database
sections.what: Compares the existing project with the PRIS record. With --force it overwrites many fields. Without it, it only fills empty fields, and it fixes plants marked Permanent Shutdown that are still listed as operating.
sections.why: The comments say fill-if-empty keeps rows that were already corrected and keeps analyst edits.
sections.watch_out: Without force, a wrong value already in the database stays, and with force, analyst edits to these fields are overwritten.

sections.name: main (part 3)
sections.title: Saves changes or inserts a new plant
sections.what: If an existing plant has changes, it saves them and counts it as updated, otherwise it counts it as skipped. For a new reactor it creates a project with the next p-number and a description naming the technology and country.
sections.why: Reason not stated for the exact insert values; they come from the mappings above.
sections.watch_out: A missing construction start date is stored as the text TBD in a date field, so the app may show odd dates.

sections.name: main: if
sections.title: Optionally links companies
sections.what: When the link flag is on, it runs company linking for the reactor and adds the number of links to the total.
sections.why: Reason stated by the flag check: linking happens only when asked for, so it is opt-in.
sections.watch_out: This runs after the project is saved, so an error here stops the run and leaves the remaining reactors unprocessed.

summary: A script that reads IAEA PRIS reactor data from a local JSON file and adds or updates matching projects in the database, and can also link owners and operators by country.
purpose: Keeps the project list in step with the IAEA Power Reactor Information System, a public reactor database.
why: The comments record a decision that the grid date means first grid connection, and that a reconciliation script exists for older rows. The country and owner mappings are likely there to fill in ownership, which PRIS does not supply.
how: It reads the command flags, loads the seed JSON file, and loads all existing projects into memory. For each reactor it looks for a match by PRIS id, then by name and country. It updates matches according to the flags, or inserts a new project with the next p-number. If asked, it links companies, then prints totals and exits.
inputs: The file seed_data/pris_reactors.json next to the script, the command flags --force, --link-companies, and --limit=N, and the projects and company-project link tables.
outputs: New or changed rows in the projects table and company-project links, plus console output with counts of inserted, updated, and skipped records and the total project count.
risks: Without --force it only fills empty fields, so wrong existing values stay. With --force it overwrites many fields, including status, dates, and attributes. Company links use hardcoded IDs, so a changed ID links the wrong company. Each reactor is saved one at a time with no transaction, so a failure part-way leaves some rows changed. A grid date is stored in the commercial operation date field.
debug: Run with --limit=5 first and read the INSERTED and UPDATED lines. Check that the seed file path resolves, since the script reads it from its own folder. If --limit is not a number, the run processes nothing. For wrong owners or operators, check the country map and the name patterns. For failed runs, read the message printed by the final error handler.
